html:
The Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act of 1856 made it legal for Hindu widows in British India to marry again. It was passed on 26 July 1856, a year before the Indian Rebellion.

Among higher caste Hindus a widow was expected never to remarry. Child marriage meant some widows were girls who had barely known their husbands. They lived on in their in laws' homes, often in hardship, heads shaved and barred from festivals.

The Bengali scholar Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar led the campaign. He argued from the ancient law books that remarriage was allowed, and gathered petitions. Orthodox leaders sent a counter petition with even more names. The government sided with the reformers.

The act was limited. A widow who remarried lost any right to her late husband's property. The first marriage under it took place in Calcutta in December 1856, with Vidyasagar's help, but few followed for decades.

It stands in a line of reforms that began when sati was banned in 1829 and ran on to the Hindu Code Bills of the 1950s, and it came out of the same Bengal Renaissance.
